strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting problem: adaptively allocating extra depth to 'harder' tokens via nested reprocessing within the same transformer layer, unifying ideas from token pruning/MoE-style routing and latent test-time scaling.

Unlike prior related work (MOR, ITT) which is limited to small (~1B) from-scratch pretrained models, this method is demonstrated as a lightweight post-training addition that scales up to a 30B-A3B MoE model, which is a practically appealing property.

The two proposed training-stability mechanisms (router controlling loss with dispersion/preservation terms, and buffer-based threshold control with EMA synchronization) are reasonably well-motivated and supported by clear ablations (Table 2) and training-dynamics plots (Fig. 4a/4b, Fig. 5) showing they reduce oscillation and better hit target selection ratios.
Reasonably broad evaluation suite (17 benchmarks across general knowledge, math/STEM, and coding/agent tasks) with consistent, if small, improvements and no reported regressions.

Interesting qualitative/interpretability analysis (layer-wise selection ratio patterns, token highlighting on QA/math/code examples) that gives some insight into what the router is learning to select.
Claimed added parameter/compute cost is small (0.03M extra parameters, ~6% FLOPs overhead per the appendix analysis), suggesting a favorable efficiency profile if the gains are real.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the two most closely related methods (MOR, ITT) or against simpler alternative baselines (e.g., uniformly adding real extra layers, naive random token selection, or a compute-matched deeper model). Table 4 only offers a qualitative feature comparison with MOR, not results on the same benchmarks/model scale, which makes it hard to judge whether DND's specific design choices (fusion strategy, threshold control) are actually superior to simpler alternatives at comparable added compute.

The reported gains are quite modest (+0.87 average on Qwen3-30B-A3B, +1.88 on Qwen3-1.7B) relative to the SFT baseline, and no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, so it is unclear whether these differences are statistically meaningful, especially for benchmarks known to have high run-to-run variance (e.g., AIME24, GPQA-Diamond).

The detailed architectural/training-strategy ablations (Table 2) are only conducted on the small Qwen3-1.7B model; it is not verified whether the same hyperparameter choices (ratio, layer range, loss weights) or the relative importance of RC/TC components hold at the 30B MoE scale actually used for the main results.

The FLOPs overhead analysis in the appendix is a theoretical back-of-envelope calculation rather than measured wall-clock latency/throughput, so real-world inference cost (which matters greatly for a method motivated by 'efficiency') is not empirically demonstrated; the added sequential recomputation within a layer could hurt latency/parallelism more than the FLOPs estimate suggests.

The core mechanism (token-choice routing + per-token threshold + reprocessing through the same layer) is conceptually a fairly incremental extension of existing MoD/MoR/ITT-style approaches; the main claimed novelty (fusion gating, router/threshold control losses) is somewhat narrow given the modest performance gains it produces.

The qualitative visualizations (Figs. 6b, 7, 8) are anecdotal (single examples) rather than systematic/quantitative evidence for the claimed interpretability finding of 'hierarchical' shallow-vs-deep token selection.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., appendix mistakenly refers to the method as 'Drop-and-Drop' instead of Dynamic Nested Depth) suggest limited proofreading, and some implementation/reproducibility details (e.g., exact SFT data composition, full search over layer ranges) are relegated to a fairly thin appendix.

strengths: The core idea of combining token-level difficulty routing with latent-space recurrent depth, applied as a lightweight post-training method rather than requiring training from scratch, is a reasonable and practically appealing direction.

The paper proposes a plausible engineering solution to a real problem (unstable/imprecise token-choice selection ratio) via a router controlling loss (dispersion + preservation) and a threshold control scheme (buffer proportional control + EMA), and provides some training dynamics plots (Fig. 4a/4b, Fig. 5) showing these components reduce oscillation relative to z-loss-only baselines.
Experiments span both a small dense model (Qwen3-1.7B) and a large MoE model (Qwen3-30B-A3B), and cover a fairly broad set of benchmarks (general, math, coding).
Qualitative visualizations of selected tokens offer some interpretability, suggesting the router focuses on semantically critical tokens (numbers, key verbs, logical connectors).
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the explicitly identified closest prior works, MOR and ITT, or against MoD — the paper only compares DND vs. vanilla SFT and ablates its own internal components. Claims of superiority over z-loss-based control (Sec 2.2, Table 4) are argued qualitatively but never validated by actually running MOR/ITT/MoD as baselines in the same post-training setting, making the central novelty claim (superior ratio control) unsubstantiated empirically.

The reported gains are very small (0.87% average on the 30B MoE model, with per-benchmark deltas often under 1 point) and are reported from what appears to be a single training run with no seeds, variance, or statistical significance testing. Given known SFT run-to-run variance, it is unclear whether these differences are meaningful versus noise.

Reproducibility is weak: the SFT training data is described only vaguely ("a significant volume of synthetic material built upon a high-quality seed set of 1-2 million instances curated from human annotations and open-source materials") with no public release, exact composition, or size breakdown, making it impossible to verify whether gains stem from DND or from this undisclosed proprietary data mixture.

The ablation study (Table 2) is only conducted on the small Qwen3-1.7B model; none of the architecture/hyperparameter ablations (RC, TC, ktarget, layer range) are validated on the larger 30B MoE model where the headline result is reported, so it is unclear the same design choices transfer to the larger/sparser setting.

The computational overhead analysis in Appendix A is an analytical/theoretical FLOPs estimate rather than measured wall-clock latency/throughput, and it inconsistently refers to the method as "Drop-and-Drop (DND)" rather than "Dynamic Nested Depth," suggesting insufficient proofreading/care in this section and raising doubts about the rigor of the efficiency claims made throughout the abstract ("minimal computing increase").
The qualitative token-selection analysis (Figs. 6b, 7, 8) is based on single anecdotal examples rather than a systematic, quantitative study, limiting the strength of the interpretability claims.

The method introduces a fairly large number of new hyperparameters (λsd, λdp, α, γ, Nb, β initialization, ktarget, Ls:Le) with limited sensitivity analysis beyond a coarse grid on the small model, raising concerns about tuning burden and robustness when applied to new models/architectures.

The reference comparisons to Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B "Non-Thinking" models in Table 1 are not well controlled (different base checkpoints/training data) and their inclusion mainly serves as a loose sanity check rather than a rigorous baseline, which can make the overall improvement narrative appear more favorable than it is.

strengths: The core idea of combining token-level difficulty-based selection with latent-space depth recurrence is a reasonable and intuitively motivated extension beyond binary token pruning, and is well-motivated conceptually in the introduction.

The method is designed as a lightweight post-training addition applicable to off-the-shelf pretrained models, which is practically appealing compared to approaches like MOR that require training from scratch.
The paper validates the approach at two different scales (1.7B dense and 30B-A3B MoE), which is a nontrivial engineering effort and shows some generality across architecture types.

The training strategy design (score dispersion loss + distribution preservation loss, buffer proportional control + EMA threshold synchronization) is reasonably well-motivated and supported by clear ablations (Table 2) and training dynamics plots (Fig. 4, 5) showing the intended regulatory effects.

The token-selection visualizations (Fig. 6, 7, 8) provide an interesting qualitative story about hierarchical processing (shallow layers selecting entities, deeper layers selecting relational/logical tokens), adding some interpretability value.
A FLOPs-based overhead analysis is provided to contextualize the computation/performance trade-off.
weaknesses: The reported performance gains are quite small (average +0.87% on the 30B MoE model, +1.88% on the 1.7B model), and no variance, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing is provided anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether these gains are reliable versus noise, especially since many individual benchmark deltas are well under 1 point.

Despite explicitly positioning MOR and ITT as the most closely related works and discussing their differences in detail (Sec. 2.2, Appendix Table 4), the paper provides no direct empirical comparison against these baselines (or against MoD) on the same benchmarks/models — the comparison is purely qualitative/architectural, which significantly weakens the claim of superiority.

There is no ablation isolating whether the gains come specifically from the token-selection/nested-depth mechanism versus simply from the extra parameters (router) or extra effective compute/training the DND-augmented model receives; a natural baseline such as applying extra generic compute (e.g., additional generic layer recurrence without selection, or longer SFT) is missing.

No wall-clock latency/throughput measurements are reported to substantiate the claimed efficiency; the overhead analysis in Appendix A is a theoretical FLOPs calculation for a 16k-token pretraining-style scenario, which is inconsistent with the actual post-training SFT experimental setting used in the main results, creating a mismatch between the efficiency claims and the empirical evaluation setting.

Key architectural hyperparameters (Ls=4, Le=43 for the 30B model; fusion weighting via β·p^i) are tuned via ablation on the small 1.7B model and then directly transferred to the 30B model without validation that this transfer is optimal, raising concerns about whether reported gains at the larger scale are near the best achievable configuration.

The SFT training data used is proprietary/custom synthetic data without public release details, which combined with the lack of code/checkpoint availability statements raises reproducibility concerns.

The paper lacks comparison to simpler strong baselines that allocate extra computation uniformly (e.g., a slightly deeper model with equivalent total FLOPs) to verify that selective/dynamic allocation is actually better than naive uniform allocation of the same extra compute budget.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated design that combines adaptive token selection with latent-space recurrent depth, addressing a real inefficiency in uniform-depth processing of tokens with varying difficulty.

The method is a practical, plug-and-play post-training approach that can be applied directly to off-the-shelf pretrained models (dense and MoE), avoiding the prohibitive cost of pretraining from scratch that limits prior work like MOR.
Demonstrated scalability across a wide range of model sizes/architectures: Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.2-1B, Gemma3-1B (dense) and Qwen3-30B-A3B (MoE), which is a meaningful engineering achievement.
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of the router controlling loss and threshold control scheme, along with layer-range and selection-ratio sensitivity analyses.

Rich interpretability analysis (token entropy correlation, logit entropy reduction after nested pass, layer-wise selection patterns, qualitative visualizations on math/code/QA) that supports the claimed mechanism of the model preferentially reprocessing uncertain/critical tokens.
Reasonable efficiency accounting, including a FLOPs overhead estimate (~6%) and measured throughput (91–93% of vanilla speed), suggesting the method is computationally lightweight.
weaknesses: The most directly relevant baseline, Mixture-of-Depths (Raposo et al., 2024), which strongly inspired the routing/fusion design, is discussed extensively but never empirically compared against in the main experiments; only ITT is used as a baseline, and only for one of the three dense models (Qwen3-1.7B).

MoE results are quite modest (average +0.87 across 17 benchmarks), with several per-benchmark gains under 0.3-0.5 points (e.g., BBH +0.13, MATH +0.15); no variance/multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess whether these small gains are statistically meaningful.

No comparison against simpler alternative baselines that would isolate the source of improvement, e.g., simply adding real extra (non-shared) layers under an equivalent compute/parameter budget, or a static/random token selection baseline, to verify the gains come from the adaptive/critical-token routing rather than merely additional average compute per token.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core architecture largely recombines existing ideas (MoD-style token routing, shared-weight recurrent/looped transformer computation), with the main contributions being engineering refinements to routing stability (entropy dispersion + MSE preservation losses, buffer/EMA threshold control) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Hyperparameters (β initialization, λ_sd, λ_dp, buffer size, α, γ, layer range) are tuned via ablation on a single small model (Qwen3-1.7B) and then directly reused for the very different 30B MoE model without independent validation, raising questions about generalization of these settings.

The FLOPs overhead analysis in the appendix is a theoretical/formal calculation rather than an empirically measured training-time FLOPs comparison, and the appendix confusingly refers to the method as "Drop-and-Drop" rather than "Dynamic Nested Depth," suggesting insufficient proofreading.

No exploration of failure cases, worst-case behavior, or tasks where DND might hurt performance, despite claiming performance gains are consistent "without any degradation"; a more critical discussion of limitations beyond generic future-work statements would strengthen the submission.
Code is stated as "to be released" without further detail, limiting immediate reproducibility given the complexity of the routing/threshold control machinery.

strengths: The core idea of combining token-level critical selection with latent recurrent depth is a reasonable and intuitive extension of mixture-of-depths and latent test-time scaling ideas, and is well-motivated in the introduction.

The paper proposes a complete architectural solution (routing, nested pass, normalized fusion) along with two dedicated training strategies (score dispersion/distribution preservation router loss and buffer-based threshold control with EMA synchronization) that address concrete stability issues of token-choice routing.
Experiments span multiple model families (Qwen3, Llama3.2, Gemma3) and scales (1B dense to 30B-A3B MoE), which is a reasonably broad evaluation for a post-training plug-in method.
The ablation study (Table 4) isolates the contribution of router control vs. threshold control and sweeps selection ratio and layer range, providing some insight into design choices.

The token-selection analysis (entropy correlation, logit-entropy reduction after nested pass, layer-wise selection patterns, qualitative visualizations on math/code) offers interpretability and partially supports the core hypothesis that the router selects genuinely 'difficult' tokens.
The method is presented as a lightweight, plug-and-play post-training addition with minimal parameter overhead, which is practically appealing if the claims hold.
weaknesses: The performance gains shrink substantially with scale: +1.88 to +2.61 on 1B dense models but only +0.87 average on the 30B-A3B MoE model, raising doubts about whether the method's benefits persist or are worthwhile at larger, more realistic scales where it would actually need to compete with simply adding parameters/compute elsewhere.

No comparison to directly relevant and closely discussed baselines: although the paper spends a full subsection and an appendix table contrasting itself with MOR, no empirical comparison to MOR (or to vanilla Mixture-of-Depths/Raposo et al.) is actually run; ITT is only compared on a single model (Qwen3-1.7B), not on Llama, Gemma, or the MoE model, making the claimed superiority over baselines thin and inconsistent across experiments.

There is no baseline that simply adds equivalent extra depth/parameters uniformly (e.g., a few extra transformer layers or uniform looped recurrence) to isolate whether the gains come from dynamic *selection* specifically, versus just the extra compute/depth itself — this is a critical missing ablation for the paper's central claim.

Inference throughput actually decreases (91.6%-93.1% of baseline speed) despite the narrative emphasizing 'minimal computing increase'; the FLOPs analysis in the appendix is a back-of-envelope estimate for a different (pretraining/MoE) configuration than most main experiments, and doesn't match the actual measured slowdown, undermining the efficiency claims.

Reproducibility is weak: code is not released ('Codes will be released soon'), training data is proprietary/synthetic and not described in enough detail to reproduce, and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported despite relatively modest absolute gains (e.g., 0.87% on MoE could be within noise).

The appendix mistakenly refers to the method as 'Drop-and-Drop (DND) policy' rather than 'Dynamic Nested Depth,' and the FLOPs analysis section appears to be a somewhat disconnected add-on (different sequence length/model configuration than the main experiments), suggesting insufficient editing care and reducing confidence in the rigor of the supplementary analysis.

The training recipe introduces many additional hyperparameters (λsd, λdp, α, γ, Nb, ktarget, Ls, Le, β initialization) that are tuned per model/setting, raising concerns about the generality and practical ease of applying DND to new models without extensive re-tuning.

The method is only validated via post-training SFT improvements on standard benchmarks; there is no analysis of whether gains hold under different fine-tuning data scales, out-of-distribution tasks, or alignment with RLHF/preference-tuning pipelines commonly used in practice.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of token-level adaptive computation (selective token recurrence) with a plug-and-play post-training recipe, avoiding the need for costly from-scratch pretraining unlike related work (MOR).

The two proposed control mechanisms (router controlling loss for score dispersion/preservation, and threshold control via buffer proportional control + EMA synchronization) are clearly motivated, theoretically reasonable, and empirically validated with clean ablations (Table 4, Figs. 5-6) showing each component contributes to performance and training stability.

Broad empirical validation across diverse model families and scales (Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.2-1B, Gemma3-1B dense models, and Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE), with consistent improvements across 17 benchmarks spanning language, math, and coding domains.
Thoughtful efficiency analysis: FLOPs overhead (~6.27%) and real-world throughput measurements (91.6-93.1% relative speed) are reported, giving a realistic picture of the cost/benefit tradeoff.

Interesting interpretability analysis (entropy correlation with token selection, layer-wise selection patterns, qualitative visualizations on math/code examples) that supports the core motivating hypothesis that DND targets genuinely difficult/uncertain tokens.
Clear and detailed writeup of architecture (routing, nested depth computation, fusion) and training strategy with explicit equations, aiding reproducibility of the method itself.
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparison: MOR, described as the "most closely related" method, is only discussed qualitatively (Appendix Table 6) and never empirically compared on benchmarks; only ITT is empirically compared, and only on a single model (Qwen3-1.7B).

The fairness/isolation of the comparison in Table 1 is unclear — it is not explicit whether the "Qwen3-1.7B" row reflects a vanilla SFT run with identical data/compute budget as the "+DND" run, which is important to rule out the possibility that gains stem from extra training signal/compute rather than the DND mechanism specifically.

No compute/parameter-matched control baseline (e.g., simply adding more standard transformer depth or more SFT steps consuming similar extra FLOPs) to isolate whether the selective nested-depth mechanism is responsible for gains versus just additional computation during post-training.

Absolute performance gains, especially for the 30B-A3B MoE model (+0.87% average), are relatively modest, and no variance/statistical significance across multiple runs is reported to assess whether such gains are robust versus noise.

Reproducibility is limited: training data is a proprietary mixture of "synthetic material" and "human-curated" seed data without public release or detailed composition, and code is only promised ("will be released soon"), making independent verification difficult.

Evidence for the qualitative claims (e.g., Fig. 4a entropy correlation, r=0.3359) is only moderately strong statistically, and conclusions drawn from it (e.g., hierarchical processing claims in Fig. 7b) rely on a single qualitative example rather than systematic quantitative analysis.

The ablation and ratio/layer-range hyperparameter studies are conducted only on the smallest dense model (Qwen3-1.7B) and then directly transferred to the 30B MoE model without re-validation at that scale, leaving open whether the chosen hyperparameters are optimal for larger/sparser architectures.
